mappings.note: Elaborating on Kitty as a trusted friend is exactly the invented-listener question LO-4 names; LO-3 would cover why she began the diary at all.
Two reasons that make Mr Keesing's displeasure reasonable - his expectations as an old-fashioned teacher. Character in context, LO-2.
Comment on the relationship between the two, which means weighing both characters across the chapter - LO-2, not a retrievable fact.
Why 'getting things off your chest' helps is the reasoned defence of writing things down that LO-5 names, applied beyond Anne's own case.
Malformed duplicate of the previous item - its stem has swallowed the earlier answer - but the question asked is the same therapeutic-writing justification, LO-5.
'The necessity of talking' is the brief Mr Keesing set, stated in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
'A Chatterbox' is named in the text; single-fact retrieval, LO-1.
Calling her father 'the most adorable' is Anne's judgement of him, so this reads her feeling towards a character (LO-2) rather than a neutral fact.
She opens with an introduction so her imagined reader can follow her - the same invented-listener reasoning as the family-sketch items, LO-4.
Her mother's name is given in the family sketch; retrieval, LO-1.
The two months of the move to Holland are stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Mrs Kuperus is named as the headmistress; single-fact retrieval.
The year of her grandmother's death is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
The date of the first entry is printed in the diary; retrieval, LO-1, not a question about why she started.
How the third essay ended the punishments is narrated in full; information extraction, LO-1.
The weight of the question is the change in the teacher's attitude, which has to be traced across the episode - LO-2.
A character sketch of Anne built around two named traits. LO-2 covers character analysis; LO-3 would require quoted evidence.
Assembles the stated facts about Mr Keesing and the punishments he set. Retrieval, LO-1, as against the 'comment on the relationship' item, which is LO-2.
Goes beyond her feelings to ask whether her portraits are fair or biased - judging the narrator's own values, LO-2.
Focuses on how Mr Keesing came round, which is character change in context, LO-2.
Most parts retrieve what Anne was doing and what her essay argued (LO-1); one part asks the learner to identify the form the extract corresponds to, a question about literary convention (C-E1.4).
'Why does Anne want to keep a diary' is LO-3; identifying the long-awaited friend as the diary she calls Kitty is the invented listener, LO-4.
Write a dated first-person post in Anne's voice. LO-6 names exactly this - producing one's own dated entry in her tone and format - even though the medium is recast as a blog.
Why it was fortunate that Mr Keesing took the joke well requires inferring what could otherwise have followed - context and consequence, LO-2.
Explains the idiom 'quaking in its boots' and then applies it to the class. Word and phrase meaning, C-E1.1.
Sanne's help with the verse is stated in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Names the third essay and what came of it - both stated; retrieval, LO-1.
Explains what Anne means by calling teachers 'the most unpredictable creatures'. Interpreting an expression, C-E1.1; this frame has no expression-matching LO.
The facts about her father (age at marriage, the move in 1933) are in the sketch; retrieval, LO-1.
Anne's rapport with her teachers is about relationships across the chapter, so LO-2 rather than a single retrievable fact.
Both halves are stated: she talked too much, and he set the 'Chatterbox' essay. Retrieval, LO-1.
The arguments of the first essay are reported in the text; extraction, LO-1.
The betting over who would move up a form is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
Weighs the title of 'The Ball Poem' against what the poem actually does - appreciation of a literary choice, which only C-E1.4 covers in this frame.
Explains what 'money is external' means in the poem. Interpreting a phrase, C-E1.1, rather than stating the poem's whole message.
What the boy is learning behind his desperate eyes is the poet's message about loss and responsibility, LO-2.
First half glosses the quoted words (C-E1.1); second half asks why the poet rejects that consolation, which is his message, LO-2.
Identifies the boy's state of mind and its cause - the persona's grief, LO-2, which is not restricted to prose.
The theme of a poem. LO-1 names theme but is worded for prose extracts, so the competency C-E1.4 is the honest fit for verse.
'What does show that' requires the learner to produce the lines that prove the ball mattered - textual evidence, LO-3.
